# The Fourier-adjoint formulation {#sec-fourier-adjoint}

## The physical question {#sec-fourier-adjoint-question}

@sec-spectral-rte left a differential equation in position and time and an
integral equation in direction. At one wavelength, with the index $\lambda$
dropped for the rest of this chapter,
$$
\left[\frac{1}{v}\partial_t+\hat{\mathbf s}\cdot\nabla
+\mu_t-\mu_s\mathcal K_g\right]I=q .
$$ {#eq-adjoint-starting-point}
Nothing about @eq-adjoint-starting-point says how to compute with it, and the
obvious reading is discouraging: $I$ has seven arguments, an event has
$10^5$–$10^6$ emitting elements, and an array has thousands of modules.

Two properties of the medium make the problem far smaller than it looks, and
this chapter is about extracting both. The medium is homogeneous and
stationary, so transforming in position and time turns streaming into
multiplication and leaves an *independent* algebraic problem on the sphere of
directions for each $(\mathbf k,\omega)$ — nothing couples one wavenumber to
another, or one frequency to another. And the operator that remains is
symmetric in the right pairing, so the roles of source and detector can be
exchanged: one solve whose right-hand side is the *detector* answers for a
whole family of sources, instead of one solve per source.

That second point is the one worth stating plainly, because it is what the
package is built on. A direct solve answers one source. An adjoint solve
answers one detector functional. After a single adjoint solve, the response to
any angular source shape is an integral against the field already computed.

## Assumptions and definitions {#sec-fourier-adjoint-assumptions}

The medium is homogeneous, stationary and unbounded, as in
@sec-spectral-rte; the solution is the causal one, with no light before the
source turns on, and boundary terms at infinity vanish. The source $q$ and the
detector functional $a$ of @sec-optical-module are both linear in the field.

The transform used throughout the book is
$$
\tilde u(\mathbf k,\omega)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\!\mathrm d^3x
\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\!\mathrm dt\;u(\mathbf x,t)\,
e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x+i\omega t},
$$ {#eq-transform-forward}
with the inverse
$$
u(\mathbf x,t)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^4}\int\!\mathrm d^3k\,\mathrm d\omega\;
\tilde u(\mathbf k,\omega)\,e^{+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-i\omega t}.
$$ {#eq-transform-inverse}
Note the opposite signs in space and in time: this is the convention the code
uses, and every phase in the package follows from it. A tilde always means
@eq-transform-forward and nothing else; a hat always means a unit vector, never
a transform.

| Symbol | Meaning | Units |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $\mathbf k$ | spatial wavenumber | $\mathrm m^{-1}$ |
| $k=\lvert\mathbf k\rvert$, $\hat{\mathbf k}=\mathbf k/k$ | magnitude and direction | $\mathrm m^{-1}$, — |
| $\omega$ | angular frequency | $\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{ns}^{-1}$ |
| $\mu=\hat{\mathbf k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf s}$ | streaming cosine | dimensionless |
| $d_0=\mu_t-i\omega/v$ | frequency-dependent part of the multiplier | $\mathrm m^{-1}$ |
| $h$ | adjoint field, $Lh=a$ | $\mathrm m$ |

### The shift theorem {#sec-fourier-adjoint-shift}

Substituting $\mathbf x'=\mathbf x-\mathbf x_0$ and $t'=t-t_0$ in
@eq-transform-forward gives, immediately,
$$
q(\mathbf x-\mathbf x_0,\;t-t_0)\;\longrightarrow\;
e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x_0+i\omega t_0}\,\tilde q(\mathbf k,\omega).
$$ {#eq-shift-theorem}
Three consequences run through the whole package. Where an emitting element
sits and when it fires do not change the medium operator: translations multiply
the transformed source by a phase. Angular source shape, source orientation and
the detector functional still enter the angular contraction and are not encoded
by @eq-shift-theorem. What is reused is the transformed medium response, not one
geometry-specific final answer. The time phase carries a **plus** sign,
$e^{+i\omega t_0}$, which is the opposite of the spatial one; a solver written
with the other time convention would produce a pulse running backwards and
would still pass any check that looks only at the charge.

## Derivation {#sec-fourier-adjoint-derivation}

Apply @eq-transform-forward to @eq-adjoint-starting-point term by term. For
the time derivative, integrating by parts and discarding the boundary term for
a field that vanishes at large $\lvert t\rvert$,
$$
\int\partial_tu\;e^{i\omega t}\,\mathrm dt
=-\int u\,\partial_t\!\left(e^{i\omega t}\right)\mathrm dt
=-i\omega\,\tilde u,
$$
and for the gradient, in the same way,
$$
\int\nabla u\;e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,\mathrm d^3x
=-\int u\,\nabla\!\left(e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\right)\mathrm d^3x
=+i\mathbf k\,\tilde u .
$$
So
$$
\partial_t\;\longrightarrow\;-i\omega,\qquad
\nabla\;\longrightarrow\;+i\mathbf k,
$$ {#eq-derivative-signs}
and the two streaming terms become
$-i\omega/v$ and $i\mathbf k\cdot\hat{\mathbf s}=ik\mu$.

The direction argument is untouched by the transform, because
@eq-transform-forward integrates over position and time only. What remains at
each $(\mathbf k,\omega)$ is an equation on the sphere,
$$
(D-V)\,\tilde I=\tilde q ,
$$ {#eq-adjoint-system}
with
$$
D(\hat{\mathbf s})=d_0+ik\mu,\qquad d_0=\mu_t-\frac{i\omega}{v},
$$ {#eq-multiplier}
$$
(Vf)(\hat{\mathbf s})=\mu_s\int_{S^2}p_g(\hat{\mathbf s},\hat{\mathbf s}')\,
f(\hat{\mathbf s}')\,\mathrm d\Omega' .
$$ {#eq-scattering-V}

Four properties of @eq-adjoint-system are the whole point of having written
it. In the homogeneous, stationary model, $D$ is a **multiplication** operator:
it multiplies the field at each direction by a complex number and mixes no
directions. $V$ acts on the direction argument alone, at fixed $\mathbf k$ and
$\omega$. Different $\mathbf k$ are not coupled, and different $\omega$ are not
coupled. The derivative mappings themselves are general, but spatially or
temporally varying optical coefficients would become convolutions and would
destroy this decoupling. Homogeneity and stationarity are therefore what make
$10^{5}$ source elements and $10^{3}$ modules share one family of solves indexed
by $(\mathbf k,\omega)$ alone.

Write $L=D-V$ for the operator of @eq-adjoint-system. It acts on functions on
the sphere, it has units of $\mathrm m^{-1}$, and it depends on
$(\mathbf k,\omega)$ but on nothing else about the problem.

### Two pairings, and why they must not be mixed {#sec-fourier-adjoint-pairings}

$L$ is complex. Two different pairings are used with it, for two different
purposes, and confusing them is the easiest mistake available here.

**The Hermitian product, for invertibility.** Let
$$
(f,g)_H=\int_{S^2}f^{*}(\hat{\mathbf s})\,g(\hat{\mathbf s})\,\mathrm d\Omega,
\qquad \|f\|^2=(f,f)_H .
$$ {#eq-hermitian-pairing}
Take $h$ and compute the real part of $(h,Lh)_H$. The multiplier contributes
$$
\operatorname{Re}\int|h|^2\left(\mu_t-\frac{i\omega}{v}+ik\mu\right)\mathrm d\Omega
=\mu_t\,\|h\|^2 ,
$$
because $-i\omega/v$ and $ik\mu$ multiply the non-negative real quantity
$|h|^2$ by something purely imaginary: **streaming contributes nothing to the
real part**, whatever $k$ and $\omega$ are. The scattering term is bounded by
$$
\left|(h,Vh)_H\right|\le\mu_s\|h\|^2 ,
$$
because $V/\mu_s$ is an integral operator with a real symmetric non-negative
kernel normalised by @eq-phase-normalisation, so its spectral radius is at most
one. Subtracting,
$$
\operatorname{Re}\,(h,Lh)_H\ \ge\ (\mu_t-\mu_s)\,\|h\|^2=\mu_a\,\|h\|^2 .
$$ {#eq-coercivity}
This is the statement that makes the whole scheme well posed, and it is worth
reading carefully for what it does *not* say. It is not enough that $\mu_t>0$:
the scattering term can cancel almost all of it, and what survives is exactly
the absorption. With $\mu_a>0$ the operator is invertible uniformly in
$\mathbf k$ and $\omega$, with $\|L^{-1}\|\le1/\mu_a$. With $\mu_a=0$ the bound
collapses, and at $k=0$, $\omega=0$ it collapses completely: there
$L=\mu_s(1-\mathcal K_g)$, and a direction-independent $h$ satisfies
$\mathcal K_gh=h$, so $Lh=0$. A purely scattering medium has an isotropic zero
mode at zero wavenumber and zero frequency, which is nothing more than the
statement that photons are then conserved and a uniform photon gas is a steady
state.

**The bilinear pairing, for reciprocity.** Now define, *without* conjugation,
$$
\langle f,g\rangle_B=\int_{S^2}f(\hat{\mathbf s})\,g(\hat{\mathbf s})\,
\mathrm d\Omega .
$$ {#eq-bilinear-pairing}
Because $D$ is a multiplication operator, moving it from one factor to the
other is trivial for any complex multiplier at all:
$$
\langle f,Dg\rangle_B=\int fDg\,\mathrm d\Omega=\int (Df)g\,\mathrm d\Omega
=\langle Df,g\rangle_B .
$$
For $V$ it follows from one property of the medium, that the phase function is
reciprocal,
$$
p_g(\hat{\mathbf s},\hat{\mathbf s}')=p_g(\hat{\mathbf s}',\hat{\mathbf s}),
$$ {#eq-phase-reciprocity}
which Henyey--Greenstein satisfies because it depends on the directions only
through $\hat{\mathbf s}\cdot\hat{\mathbf s}'$. Then, renaming the integration
variables,
$$
\langle f,Vg\rangle_B=\mu_s\iint f(\hat{\mathbf s})\,
p_g(\hat{\mathbf s},\hat{\mathbf s}')\,g(\hat{\mathbf s}')
=\langle Vf,g\rangle_B ,
$$
and therefore
$$
L^{T}=L,\qquad (L^{-1})^{T}=L^{-1}
$$ {#eq-complex-symmetric}
in the bilinear pairing.

The distinction is worth one more sentence because it is not a technicality.
$L$ is **complex symmetric**: $L^T=L$. It is **not** Hermitian: $L^\dagger\ne L$
whenever $\omega\ne0$ or $k\ne0$, since $D$ then has an imaginary part.
@eq-coercivity needs the Hermitian product and says nothing about transposes;
@eq-complex-symmetric needs the bilinear pairing and says nothing about norms.
A derivation that conjugates halfway through gets $L^\dagger$ where it wanted
$L^T$ and arrives at a reciprocity relation with a spurious complex
conjugate — which is invisible at $\omega=0$ and wrong everywhere else.

### Source and detector change places {#sec-fourier-adjoint-swap}

Let $q(\hat{\mathbf s})$ be the transformed angular source at this
$(\mathbf k,\omega)$ and $a(\hat{\mathbf s})$ the detector functional of
@sec-optical-module, so that the transformed response is
$$
\tilde R=\langle a,\,L^{-1}q\rangle_B .
$$ {#eq-direct-response}
Define the **adjoint field** as the solution of
$$
Lh=a .
$$ {#eq-adjoint-equation}
Then, by @eq-complex-symmetric,
$$
\tilde R=\langle a,L^{-1}q\rangle_B
=\langle (L^{-1})^{T}a,\,q\rangle_B
=\langle L^{-1}a,\,q\rangle_B
=\langle h,\,q\rangle_B .
$$ {#eq-adjoint-response}
@eq-adjoint-response is the result this chapter exists to produce. The source
has left the solve entirely: it appears only under an integral against a field
that was computed without knowing it. With $[a]$ dimensionless and
$[L]=\mathrm m^{-1}$, the adjoint field has units of metres.

Four cases show what that buys.

**An isotropic detector.** $a(\hat{\mathbf s})=1$, so $Lh=1$: one right-hand
side, no angular structure, one solve per $(\mathbf k,\omega)$.

**A directed point source.** $q(\hat{\mathbf s})
=\delta_{S^2}(\hat{\mathbf s}-\hat{\mathbf s}_0)$ gives
$$
\tilde R=h(\hat{\mathbf s}_0),
$$ {#eq-directed-evaluation}
a *evaluation* of the adjoint field. Every emission direction
$\hat{\mathbf s}_0$ is answered by reading off one value of the same $h$. This
is the sharpest form of the saving: one solve, all directions.

**An isotropic source.** $q=1/4\pi$ gives
$$
\tilde R=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{S^2}h\,\mathrm d\Omega ,
$$
one average of the same field.

**A directional module.** For a general $a(\hat{\mathbf s})$
@eq-adjoint-response is still exact, but it is one solve per right-hand side,
and a module that can point in an arbitrary direction does not present one
fixed $a$: rotating the module rotates the right-hand side. What makes that
affordable is expanding $a$ in a basis whose size is set by the angular
bandwidth $L_A$ measured in @sec-optical-module, and solving once per basis
function rather than once per orientation. **One solve does not serve arbitrary
module orientations by itself**; @sec-directional-om is where that expansion is
constructed and counted.

### Real signals and half the frequency axis {#sec-fourier-adjoint-real}

A physical response is a real function of position and time. Conjugating
@eq-transform-forward for real $u$ gives
$$
\tilde R(-\mathbf k,-\omega)=\tilde R(\mathbf k,\omega)^{*} ,
$$ {#eq-conjugate-symmetry}
so the negative frequencies carry no information the positive ones do not. This
is why the interface stores a non-negative, strictly increasing frequency axis
and why a solve is asked for $\omega\ge0$ only. The corresponding half-axis
inversion back to time bins is @sec-time-and-bins and is not derived here.

One transitional remark. @eq-adjoint-equation is an equation on the sphere and
has not been made finite: choosing an angular basis, discovering that the
operator is tridiagonal in it, and closing the infinite tail exactly are the
subject of @sec-angular-system. Everything in the present chapter is basis-free
and holds whatever that choice turns out to be.

## The discrete algorithm {#sec-fourier-adjoint-algorithm}

At the level of this chapter, one $(\mathbf k,\omega)$ is processed as follows.

1. **Fix a wavelength** and take its monochromatic coefficients
   $\mu_a,\mu_s,g,n_g$ from @sec-spectral-rte.
2. **Choose a point** $(\mathbf k,\omega)$ of the transform.
3. **Build the frequency part** $d_0=\mu_t-i\omega/v$, one complex number.
4. **Build the multiplier** $D(\hat{\mathbf s})=d_0+ik\mu$, diagonal in
   direction.
5. **Set the right-hand side** to the angular detector functional $a$.
6. **Solve** $(D-V)h=a$ for the adjoint field.
7. **Contract** with each angular source in turn,
   $\tilde R_j=\langle h,q_j\rangle_B$; every source after the first costs an
   integral and not a solve.
8. **Store** the resulting spectrum for the later inversion in space and time.

Steps 5 and 6 are where the choice of angular basis enters, and that choice is
@sec-angular-system. Step 7 is where the event geometry enters, through
@eq-shift-theorem, and nothing before step 7 knows anything about it.

## Correspondence with the code {#sec-fourier-adjoint-code}

| Mathematics | Symbol |
|:--|:--|
| $\mu_t$ | `lighthit.medium.Medium.extinction_per_m` |
| $v=c_0/n_g$ | `lighthit.medium.Medium.speed_m_per_ns` |
| $d_0=\mu_t-i\omega/v$, @eq-multiplier | `lighthit.angular.angular_components`, `lighthit.angular.resolvent_rows` |
| Eigenvalues of the scattering operator $V$ | `lighthit.angular.angular_components`, `lighthit.angular.resolvent_rows` |
| The solve for a point source | `lighthit.green.PointGreenSolver.solve` |
| Directed or isotropic source, @eq-directed-evaluation | `lighthit.green.PointGreenSolver.solve(direction=...)` |
| The transformed result $\tilde R$ | `lighthit.green.GreenResult.spectrum` |
| The frequency axis, @eq-conjugate-symmetry | `lighthit.green.GreenResult.omega_per_ns` |
| The emission-time phase $e^{+i\omega t_0}$, @eq-shift-theorem | `lighthit.green.PointGreenSolver.solve` |
| The later half-axis inversion | `lighthit.readout.inverse_bins` |

Two things this table implies are worth saying outright. `direction=None`
selects the isotropic source and a unit vector selects a directed one; the
choice changes the contraction of step 7 and not the solve of step 6, which is
exactly @eq-adjoint-response at work. And the code never allocates
$I(\mathbf x,\hat{\mathbf s},t)$ on a grid: there is no array over three
spatial coordinates, two angles and time anywhere in the package. What is
stored is a spectrum indexed by frequency and by observation point, and that
is a direct consequence of @eq-adjoint-response and @eq-shift-theorem rather
than a memory optimisation.

## A worked number {#sec-fourier-adjoint-example}

The example builds an independent dense angular discretisation — a product
quadrature on the sphere, Gauss--Legendre in $\cos\theta$ with the polar axis
along $\hat{\mathbf k}$, uniform in $\varphi$ — assembles $L$ as a matrix, and
checks the chapter's three claims against it. It is a reference for the
derivation and not the production solver, which uses a different and far
smaller representation. Public synthetic parameters only; no cache, no
compiled backend.

```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 \
NUMBA_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  python scripts/run_fourier_adjoint_example.py --output .build/fourier-adjoint-example
```

The stored output is `docs/fourier-adjoint-example/summary.json`, which carries
the configuration, the library versions, the thread settings and the exact
value of every residual quoted below as a bound.

**Configuration.** $\mu_a=0.04\ \mathrm m^{-1}$, $\mu_s=0.05\ \mathrm m^{-1}$,
$g=0.7$, $n_g=1.35$, so $\mu_t=0.09\ \mathrm m^{-1}$ and
$v=0.2220685\ \mathrm m\,\mathrm{ns}^{-1}$. The transform point is
$k=0.35\ \mathrm m^{-1}$, $\omega=0.08\ \mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{ns}^{-1}$, giving
$$
d_0=0.090000-0.360249\,i\ \ \mathrm m^{-1},
$$
which is @eq-multiplier evaluated by hand. The grid is 20 polar by 14
azimuthal nodes, 280 directions, and it integrates the sphere to $4\pi$
exactly.

**The matrix is symmetric in the weighted sense.** On a quadrature with
weights $w_i$ the bilinear pairing @eq-bilinear-pairing is $f^{T}Wg$ with
$W=\operatorname{diag}(w_i)$, and @eq-complex-symmetric becomes $WL=L^{T}W$.
The relative residual of that identity is below $10^{-14}$ — it is an algebraic
consequence of $p_g$ being symmetric, so nothing but round-off can appear in
it.

**Reciprocity, with one adjoint solve.** One detector functional --- the
quadratic acceptance of @sec-optical-module about an axis tilted away from
$\hat{\mathbf k}$, so that no azimuthal symmetry is left to hide an error ---
and four angular sources: isotropic; a forward lobe; a discrete delta at one
quadrature node; and a cosine lobe. The direct route solves $LI=q$ once per
source and contracts with $a$; the adjoint route solves $Lh=a$ **once** and
contracts with each source. The two agree to a relative error below $10^{-11}$
for every source — in this run at the level of machine precision. The discrete
delta additionally reproduces @eq-directed-evaluation: contracting it with $h$
returns the value of $h$ at that node, to the same precision.

**Coercivity.** In the weighted orthonormal representation
$B=W^{1/2}LW^{-1/2}$, the Hermitian part $H=(B+B^\dagger)/2$ has
$$
\lambda_{\min}(H)=0.0396196\ \mathrm m^{-1}
\quad\text{against}\quad \mu_a=0.04\ \mathrm m^{-1},
$$
and $\lambda_{\max}(H)=0.09\ \mathrm m^{-1}=\mu_t$. The continuous operator is
bounded below by $\mu_a$; this finite quadrature falls below that target by
$3.8\times10^{-4}$. The deficit is not a failure of the continuous bound: it is
the quadrature. The
grid does not integrate $\int p_g\,\mathrm d\Omega=1$ exactly, and the largest
residual of that normalisation on this grid is $1.5\times10^{-2}$, which caps
the deficit at $\mu_s\times1.5\times10^{-2}=7.7\times10^{-4}$. Refining the
grid confirms it:

| directions | normalisation residual | coercivity deficit | $\mu_s\times$ residual |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 120 | $7\times10^{-2}$ | $1.9\times10^{-3}$ | $3.3\times10^{-3}$ |
| 280 | $2\times10^{-2}$ | $3.8\times10^{-4}$ | $7.7\times10^{-4}$ |
| 768 | $4\times10^{-4}$ | $8.7\times10^{-6}$ | $2.2\times10^{-5}$ |
| 1280 | $3\times10^{-5}$ | $4.4\times10^{-7}$ | $1.3\times10^{-6}$ |

Note which statements depend on the grid and which do not. Reciprocity and the
weighted symmetry are algebraic identities of the discrete matrix and hold to
round-off on every grid, including the coarsest. The coercivity bound is a
statement about the continuous operator, and the discretisation approaches it
from below at the rate its quadrature normalises the phase function.

**The signs of the transform.** On a Gaussian in $x$ and a Gaussian in $t$,
with the derivatives taken analytically so that no finite-difference error
enters, @eq-derivative-signs returns $+ik$ in space and $-i\omega$ in time,
and @eq-shift-theorem returns $e^{-ikx_0}$ and $e^{+i\omega t_0}$ for a shift
of $x_0=2.5$ m and $t_0=1.75$ ns. All four errors are below $10^{-9}$; in this
run they are at round-off. The two phases are checked separately, because a
single combined test would pass with both signs flipped.

**The zero mode.** Setting $\mu_a=0$, $k=0$, $\omega=0$ --- built directly
rather than through `Medium`, whose contract requires strictly positive
absorption --- the direction-independent vector is annihilated up to exactly
the grid's normalisation error, an identity the run confirms to round-off. The
next eigenvalue is $0.01446\ \mathrm m^{-1}$, against the analytic
$\mu_s(1-g)=0.015\ \mathrm m^{-1}$: the gap above the zero mode is set by how
much the first anisotropic moment is damped, which is what will make the
truncated problem in @sec-angular-system well conditioned away from that
corner.

## Checks {#sec-fourier-adjoint-checks}

Fourteen checks are recorded as booleans in the stored summary, and the script
exits with a failure if any is false. They fall into three groups.

**Conventions.** $\partial_t\to-i\omega$ and $\nabla\to+ik$ are verified
separately; the source shift reproduces $e^{-ikx_0+i\omega t_0}$ with the
spatial and temporal phases checked apart; and $d_0$ assembled from the medium
agrees with $\mu_t-i\omega/v$ exactly.

**Algebra.** The quadrature integrates the sphere to $4\pi$ exactly; $WL=L^TW$
holds to round-off; reciprocity holds for four different sources from a single
adjoint solve; and the discrete delta evaluates the adjoint field at its node.

**Analysis.** The Hermitian part of the similarity-transformed operator has
$\lambda_{\min}\ge\mu_a$ up to the quadrature deficit, and that deficit is
required to lie inside $\mu_s$ times the measured normalisation residual of the
grid; the residual falls as the grid is refined, reaching below $10^{-3}$ on
the finest; and at $\mu_a=k=\omega=0$ the isotropic residual is *equal* to the
grid's normalisation error, which is the discrete form of the analytic
statement that the mode is exactly annihilated.

Nothing in this chapter validates the production solver. What is checked is
that the formulation is consistent and that the operator has the properties the
later chapters will assume of it.

## Range of validity {#sec-fourier-adjoint-validity}

- **Homogeneous and stationary medium.** Without it the transform does not
  decouple the wavenumbers, and @eq-adjoint-system is not one independent
  problem per $(\mathbf k,\omega)$.
- **Unbounded domain, or boundary terms that vanish.** The integrations by
  parts in @eq-derivative-signs discard surface terms.
- **The causal solution.** The transform selects the retarded solution; nothing
  here fixes a different branch.
- **Linear source and detector.** @eq-direct-response and
  @eq-adjoint-response are statements about a linear map; a detector whose
  response depends on the light already received is outside them.
- **A reciprocal scalar phase kernel.** @eq-phase-reciprocity is what makes
  $L^T=L$. A non-reciprocal kernel gives $L^T\ne L$ and
  @eq-adjoint-response fails; the adjoint field would then solve $L^Th=a$, a
  separate transpose solve, and the saving of one solve for many sources
  survives only in that modified form.
- **Real $k$ and $\omega$.** Complex wavenumbers or frequencies are not
  considered; the coercivity argument uses that $ik\mu$ and $-i\omega/v$ are
  purely imaginary.
- **$\mu_a>0$** for invertibility uniform in $(\mathbf k,\omega)$. At
  $\mu_a=0$ the bound degenerates and the isotropic zero mode at
  $k=\omega=0$ is genuine.
- **Distributions are admissible** on the right-hand side: the point impulses
  of @eq-directed-evaluation are not ordinary functions, and the pairings are
  understood in that sense.
- **Finite ranges are a later matter.** Truncating $k$, truncating $\omega$ and
  inverting numerically belong to @sec-scattering-orders and
  @sec-time-and-bins; nothing in this chapter approximates anything.

## Exercises {#sec-fourier-adjoint-exercises}

1. Derive @eq-derivative-signs from @eq-transform-forward by parts, stating
   which boundary terms are discarded and under what decay assumption. Then
   show that the *inverse* transform @eq-transform-inverse reverses both signs,
   and that the pair is consistent.
2. Derive @eq-shift-theorem by substitution, and show that reversing the sign
   convention in time turns $e^{+i\omega t_0}$ into $e^{-i\omega t_0}$ and
   sends a pulse arriving at $t_0>0$ to one arriving at $-t_0$.
3. Prove $\langle f,Lg\rangle_B=\langle Lf,g\rangle_B$ from
   @eq-phase-reciprocity, treating the multiplication and integral parts
   separately, and identify exactly where the absence of conjugation is used.
4. Exhibit an $f$ for which $(f,Lf)_H$ is not real at $\omega\ne0$, and
   conclude that $L^T=L$ does not imply $L^\dagger=L$. Then show that the two
   coincide when $k=\omega=0$.
5. Derive @eq-coercivity, justifying the bound on the scattering term from the
   normalisation @eq-phase-normalisation, and deduce
   $\|L^{-1}\|\le1/\mu_a$. Explain why $\mu_t>0$ alone gives no such bound.
6. Show that at $\mu_a=0$, $k=0$, $\omega=0$ the constant function is
   annihilated by $L$. Then compute the next eigenvalue for
   Henyey--Greenstein scattering and compare with the value measured in
   @sec-fourier-adjoint-example.
7. Derive @eq-directed-evaluation from @eq-adjoint-response, and state what
   changes if the source is a narrow but finite lobe rather than a delta.
8. Derive the isotropic-source result $\tilde R=\frac1{4\pi}\int h$, and say
   which single number of the adjoint field it requires.
9. Suppose the phase kernel is not reciprocal. Write the modified
   @eq-adjoint-response, say which operator the adjoint field now solves
   against, and state what is still reused across sources and what is not.
10. Prove @eq-conjugate-symmetry for a real response, and deduce that storing
    $\omega\ge0$ loses nothing. Then show that a half-axis store implicitly
    assumes the response really is real.
